claim: A few Cdkn1c mutant mice survived in a mixed CD1;B6 background at 4.2%
source: Although Cdkn1c loss is generally associated with perinatal death (Yan et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 1997; Susaki et al., 2009; Mademtzoglou et al., 2017), a few Cdkn1c mutant mice survived in a mixed CD1;B6 background (4.2%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited references about perinatal lethality.

claim: Cdkn1c-deficient mice displayed reduced body weight compared to control littermates
source: Cdkn1c-deficient mice displayed reduced body weight compared to control littermates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C showing body weight measurements.

claim: There was no significant difference in forelimb grip strength between Cdkn1c mutant and control mice at 1 or 2 months of age when the strength was calculated on a per weight basis
source: However, there was no significant difference in forelimb grip strength between Cdkn1c mutant and control mice at 1 or 2 months of age when the strength was calculated on a per weight basis.
evidence: The claim is supported by grip strength measurements normalized to body weight shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Strength was slightly higher in 3- or 4-month-old Cdkn1c mutant mice compared to controls
source: Strength was even slightly higher in 3- or 4-month-old Cdkn1c mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by grip strength data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cdkn1c knock-out muscles contained smaller fibers and displayed increased fibrosis
source: Histological analysis showed that Cdkn1c knock-out muscles contained smaller fibers and displayed increased fibrosis (Figure 1A–D), implying hindered myogenic differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A–D including HE and Sirius red staining.

claim: The amount of centrally located nuclei was comparable in mutants and controls
source: The amount of centrally located nuclei, indicative of ongoing regeneration, was comparable in mutants and controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 1E.

claim: The number of PAX7+ MuSC on freshly isolated myofibers of EDLs was increased in Cdkn1c mutant mice compared to the controls
source: The number of PAX7+ MuSC on freshly isolated myofibers of Extensor digitorum longus (EDLs) was increased in Cdkn1c mutant mice compared to the controls (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 1F–G.

claim: PAX7+ MuSCs on Cdkn1c mutant myofibers were mostly MYOD-, at a similar percentage to controls
source: Furthermore, PAX7+ MuSCs on Cdkn1c mutant myofibers were mostly MYOD-, at a similar percentage to controls (Figure 1H), indicating that Cdkn1c is not regulating MuSCs quiescence.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 1H and interpreted to indicate Cdkn1c does not regulate quiescence.

claim: Cdkn1c mutants displayed an increased ratio of PAX7+ MYOD- self-renewing cells and a decreased ratio of PAX7-MYOD+ differentiating myoblasts at T72
source: When single myofibers were cultured for 72 hr (T72), Cdkn1c mutants displayed an increased ratio of PAX7+ MYOD- self-renewing cells and a decreased ratio of PAX7-MYOD+ differentiating myoblasts (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 1I–J.

claim: In the absence of CDKN1c the MuSC compartment is correctly established, but a proportion of the MuSC population undergo increased self-renewal at the expense of differentiation
source: Taken together, our data suggest that in the absence of CDKN1c the MuSC compartment is correctly established, but a proportion of the MuSC population undergo increased self-renewal at the expense of differentiation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data from Figure 1 showing increased PAX7+ cells and decreased differentiation markers.

claim: At d3 post-injury, loss of Cdkn1c promoted myoblasts proliferation and counteracted differentiation
source: At d3 post-injury, loss of Cdkn1c promoted myoblasts proliferation and counteracted differentiation, as shown by increased EdU+ incorporation and reduced MYOD+EdU+ fraction, respectively. (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation and MYOD expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: At d4 post-injury, Cdkn1c-deficient muscles showed smaller embryonic myosin (eMyHC)+ myofibers compared to controls
source: At d4 post-injury, Cdkn1c-deficient muscles showed smaller embryonic myosin (eMyHC)+ myofibers, a marker for early myofiber formation, compared to controls (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by eMyHC immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 2A,C.

claim: At d7 post-injury, Cdkn1c-deficient muscles showed increased cell infiltration and smaller and heterogeneous myofiber formation
source: At d7 post-injury, Cdkn1c-deficient muscles showed increased cell infiltration and smaller and heterogeneous myofiber formation (Figure 2A,B,D), suggesting a delay in the regeneration process.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data in Figure 2A,B,D and interpreted as delayed regeneration.

claim: At d30, signs of impaired regeneration associated with smaller fibers were observed, including deposition of fibrotic tissue in Cdkn1c-mutant mice
source: At d30, signs of impaired regeneration associated with smaller fibers were observed (Figure 2A,B,E), including deposition of fibrotic tissue (Figure 2A,F) in Cdkn1c-mutant mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological and Sirius red staining data in Figure 2A,B,E,F.

claim: The number of PAX7+ MuSCs was increased in Cdkn1c mutants compared to the controls at d30 post-injury
source: The number of PAX7+ MuSCs was increased in Cdkn1c mutants compared to the controls (Figure 2G–H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 2G–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The proportion of MYOD+ MuSCs was not altered at d30 post-injury in Cdkn1c mutants
source: while the proportion of MYOD+ MuSCs was not altered (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 2I.

claim: Cdkn1c is required for postnatal muscle repair
source: Therefore, our data suggest that Cdkn1c is required for postnatal muscle repair.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the regeneration data from Figure 2 showing impaired muscle repair in Cdkn1c mutants.

claim: Cdkn1c mutant myogenic cells demonstrated increased propensity for stem-cell self-renewal during both tissue establishment and regeneration
source: In addition, Cdkn1c mutant myogenic cells demonstrated increased propensity for stem-cell self-renewal during both tissue establishment and regeneration.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of data from Figures 1 and 2 showing increased PAX7+ cells in mutants.

claim: One week of TMX administration led to 84.5% recombination efficiency in Pax7CreERT2; Cdkn1cFlox mice
source: One week of TMX administration led to 84.5% recombination efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by recombination efficiency data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Cdkn1c transcript and protein were induced by differentiation in control cells
source: Cdkn1c transcript and protein were induced by differentiation in control cells (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B–C.

claim: Cdkn1c transcript and protein were not detected in cells from mutant animals
source: In contrast, they were not detected in cells from mutant animals (Figure 3B,D), demonstrating efficient Cre-mediated recombination of the Cdkn1c allele in FACS-isolated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B,D showing absence of Cdkn1c in mutants.

claim: Primary myoblasts derived from MuSC-specific Cdkn1c mutant mice showed increased proliferation with 50% more EdU+ cells and 38% more KI67+ cells in growth conditions
source: When cells were maintained in growth conditions for 5 days, we observed 50% and 38% more EdU+ and KI67+ cells, respectively, in the absence of CDKN1c (Figure 3E–H), suggesting that CDKN1c is involved in restraining cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU and KI67 quantification data in Figure 3E–H.

claim: One-day post-differentiation, MYOGENIN was significantly decreased in FACS-isolated MuSCs from MuSC-specific Cdkn1c-deficient mice
source: One-day post-differentiation, MYOGENIN was significantly decreased (Figure 3I,K,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by MYOGENIN immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3I,K,L.

claim: Myotube formation 3 days post-differentiation was severely compromised in cultures of FACS-isolated MuSCs from MuSC-specific Cdkn1c-deficient mice
source: In addition, myotube formation 3 days post-differentiation was severely compromised (Figure 3J,M,N).
evidence: The claim is supported by MyHC immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3J,M,N.

claim: Both MuSC-specific and global ablation of CDKN1c led to increased primary myoblasts proliferation at the expense of myogenic differentiation
source: In conclusion, both MuSC-specific and global ablation of CDKN1c led to increased primary myoblasts proliferation at the expense of myogenic differentiation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of data from Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing increased proliferation and decreased differentiation.

claim: CDKN1c is required in MuSCs for correct cell cycle regulation and differentiation during postnatal myogenesis
source: Together, our data demonstrate that CDKN1c is required in MuSCs for correct cell cycle regulation and differentiation during postnatal myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined data from Figures 1-3 showing proliferation and differentiation defects.

claim: Four weeks of tamoxifen administration achieved 94.5% recombination efficiency in MuSCs of Pax7CreERT2; Cdkn1cFlox mice
source: Following 4 weeks of tamoxifen administration to induce recombination in adult (8- to 12-week-old) mice, we injected control and Pax7CreERT2/+; Cdkn1cFlox (Cdkn1c cKO) TA muscles with CTX and evaluated muscle repair at 7 days post-injury (Figure 4A), having achieved 94.5% recombination efficiency in MuSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by recombination efficiency data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Pax7CreERT2 heterozygous mice display a mild regeneration phenotype
source: Hence, in all experiments we also included Cre control mice, as we found that Pax7CreERT2 (Lepper et al., 2009) heterozygous mice display a mild regeneration phenotype (Figure 4B–G')
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data in Figure 4B–G' showing regeneration defects in Cre control mice.

claim: Cre control muscles showed increased cell infiltration and reduced regenerated myofibers of smaller sizes compared to Wt at d7 post-injury
source: In contrast, Cre control muscles showed increased cell infiltration and reduced regenerated myofibers of smaller sizes compared to Wt (Figure 4B'; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data in Figure 4B' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Muscle regeneration was severely compromised in Cdkn1c cKO muscles at d7 post-injury, in which newly formed myofibers were rare and small and most of the tissue consisted of cell infiltration and fat deposits
source: while muscle regeneration was severely compromised in Cdkn1c cKO muscles, in which newly formed myofibers were rare and small and most of the tissue consisted of cell infiltration and fat deposits (Figure 4B'', C''; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data in Figure 4B'', C'' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Induction of early differentiation was delayed in Cdkn1c cKO and Cre control muscles, as evidenced by the presence of embryonic eMyHC+ fibers at d7 post-injury
source: Furthermore, induction of early differentiation was delayed, as evidenced by the presence of embryonic eMyHC+ fibers in Cdkn1c cKO and Cre control, but not in Wt muscles at this time point (Figure 4D–E'').
evidence: The claim is supported by eMyHC immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D–E''.

claim: There was a massive diminution of the MuSC compartment in Cdkn1c cKO muscles at d7 post-injury
source: Consistent with the lack of tissue regeneration, we observed a massive diminution of the MuSC compartment in Cdkn1c cKO muscles (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAX7 immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 4F–H.

claim: CDKN1c expression in the myogenic lineage is required for muscle repair
source: Together, our data reveal that CDKN1c expression in the myogenic lineage is required for muscle repair.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the regeneration data from Figure 4 showing severe impairment in Cdkn1c cKO mice.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs were not labeled with CDKN1c antibody in single myofiber cultures
source: Immunostaining experiments, using a CDKN1c-specific antibody, showed that quiescent MuSCs were not labeled (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing absence of CDKN1c in quiescent MuSCs.

claim: MuSCs of resting adult TA muscles were CDKN1c-negative following labeling of cryosections
source: Similarly, MuSCs of resting adult TA muscles were CDKN1c-negative following labeling of cryosections (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing absence of CDKN1c in MuSCs.

claim: Activated PAX7+ and MYOD+ myoblasts at T24-T48 presented with increasing amounts of CDKN1c
source: Activated PAX7+ and MYOD+ myoblasts at T24-T48 presented with increasing amounts of CDKN1c.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5A–B and 6A–B showing CDKN1c expression in activated myoblasts.

claim: During the early proliferation phase (T24-T48), CDKN1c was restricted to the cytoplasm
source: However, during this early proliferation phase, CDKN1c was restricted to the cytoplasm (Figures 5A–B and 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5A–B and 6A–B showing cytoplasmic localization.

claim: CDKN1c was mainly restricted to the cytoplasm at d3 following CTX injection in vivo
source: Consistent with these findings, CDKN1c was mainly restricted to the cytoplasm at d3 following CTX injection in vivo, a time point when most cells are in a proliferative state (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C showing cytoplasmic CDKN1c at d3 post-injury.

claim: As differentiation proceeded (MYOD+ followed by MYOGENIN+ at T72), Cdkn1c expression became increasingly nuclear
source: Interestingly, as differentiation proceeded (MYOD+ followed by MYOGENIN +at T72), Cdkn1c expression became increasingly nuclear (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B–C showing nuclear translocation during differentiation.

claim: Cdkn1c was mostly cytoplasmic in PAX7+/Cdkn1c+ T72 myoblasts
source: Although Cdkn1c was mostly cytoplasmic in PAX7+/Cdkn1c + T72 myoblasts
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6A showing cytoplasmic localization in PAX7+ cells.

claim: Cdkn1c exhibited nuclear presence in around 25% of MYOD+/Cdkn1c+ T72 myoblasts
source: Cdkn1c exhibited nuclear presence in around 25% of MYOD+/Cdkn1c+ and 55% of MYOGENIN+/Cdkn1c + T72 myoblasts (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6B showing nuclear localization percentages.

claim: Cdkn1c exhibited nuclear presence in around 55% of MYOGENIN+/Cdkn1c+ T72 myoblasts
source: Cdkn1c exhibited nuclear presence in around 25% of MYOD+/Cdkn1c+ and 55% of MYOGENIN+/Cdkn1c + T72 myoblasts (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6C showing nuclear localization percentages.

claim: Cdkn1c protein was mainly restricted to cell nuclei at late stages of regeneration (d13 post-CTX)
source: In line with this, Cdkn1c protein was mainly restricted to cell nuclei at late stages of regeneration following in vivo muscle injury (d13 post-CTX; Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C showing nuclear CDKN1c at d13 post-injury.

claim: Cdkn1c continued to be present in KI67+ proliferating cells at T72, yet limited to their cytoplasm
source: Finally, similarly to the T24-T48 activated/cycling populations of myoblasts in single myofibers ex vivo, Cdkn1c continued to be present in KI67+ proliferating cells at T72, yet limited to their cytoplasm (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6D showing cytoplasmic CDKN1c in KI67+ cells.

claim: Cdkn1c did not show significant enrichment at MYOD-binding sites in muscle regulatory regions
source: We performed ChIP experiments with an anti-Cdkn1c antibody to test whether Cdkn1c shares these binding sites with MYOD, and we found no significant enrichment at any of the tested sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing lack of enrichment.

claim: Overexpression of full-length Cdkn1c in single myofiber cultures was associated with nuclear CDKN1c protein and a marked decrease in cycling myoblasts
source: Overexpression of Cdkn1c FL in single myofiber cultures was associated with nuclear CDKN1c protein (Figure 6E) and a marked decrease in cycling myoblasts (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6E,F showing nuclear localization and reduced proliferation.

claim: Forced expression of the NLS-deficient construct restricted CDKN1c to the cytoplasm and did not induce cell cycle exit
source: In contrast, forced expression of the NLS-deficient construct restricted CDKN1c to the cytoplasm (Figure 6E) and did not induce cell cycle exit as Cdkn1c FL (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6E,F showing cytoplasmic localization and maintained proliferation.

claim: Overexpression of either Cdkn1c FL or Cdkn1c–NLS did not alter the proportions of cells entering myogenic differentiation
source: By contrast, overexpression of either Cdkn1c FL or Cdkn1c –NLS did not alter the proportions of cells entering myogenic differentiation, as evidenced by MYOD and/or MYOGENIN expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D showing no change in differentiation markers.

claim: In Cdkn1c-deficient myoblasts, cell cycle exit was observed with Cdkn1c FL but not Cdkn1c–NLS, uncoupled from myogenic differentiation
source: Comparably to the ex vivo system of single myofibers (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D), we observed cell cycle exit, uncoupled from myogenic differentiation, in Cdkn1c FL but not Cdkn1c –NLS (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–G showing cell cycle exit without differentiation changes.

claim: Nuclear CDKN1c promotes growth arrest, while cytoplasmic localization of the protein is compatible with proliferation
source: Together, these results show that nuclear CDKN1c promotes growth arrest, while cytoplasmic localization of the protein - observed at early stages of MuSC activation - is compatible with proliferation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the retroviral overexpression data from Figure 6 showing differential effects based on localization.

claim: The data suggest uncoupling of cell cycle exit and myogenic differentiation
source: Furthermore, our data suggest uncoupling of cell cycle exit and myogenic differentiation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of data from Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing cell cycle changes without differentiation changes.

claim: MuSCs originate from PAX3/7+ progenitor cells that in late fetal life acquire their characteristic anatomical position between the basal lamina and the plasma membrane of muscle fibers
source: MuSCs originate from a PAX3/7+ progenitor cells that in late fetal life acquire their characteristic anatomical position between the basal lamina and the plasma membrane of muscle fibers (Mauro, 1961; Relaix et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MuSC origin and positioning.

claim: MuSCs are indispensable for postnatal muscle growth
source: MuSCs are indispensable for postnatal muscle growth (White et al., 2010; Pawlikowski et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MuSC function in muscle growth.

claim: MuSCs are indispensable for muscle maintenance
source: maintenance (Keefe et al., 2015; Pawlikowski et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MuSC function in muscle maintenance.

claim: MuSCs are indispensable for regeneration upon injury
source: and regeneration upon injury (Lepper et al., 2011; McCarthy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2011; Sambasivan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MuSC function in muscle regeneration.

claim: The majority of juvenile MuSCs acquire a non-proliferative, quiescent state around 3 weeks of post-natal life
source: The majority of juvenile MuSCs acquire a non-proliferative, quiescent state around 3 weeks of post-natal life to ensure cellular/genomic integrity and long-term survival (Lepper et al., 2009; White et al., 2010; Cheung and Rando, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MuSC quiescence timing and function.

claim: Once stimulated by homeostatic demand or damage, adult MuSCs exit quiescence, re-enter the cell cycle, and provide differentiated progeny for muscle repair
source: However, once stimulated by homeostatic demand or damage, adult MuSCs exit quiescence, re-enter the cell cycle, and provide differentiated progeny for muscle repair, while a subpopulation self-renews to preserve the quiescent pool (Relaix and Zammit, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about MuSC activation and function.

claim: A subpopulation of MuSCs self-renews to preserve the quiescent pool
source: while a subpopulation self-renews to preserve the quiescent pool (Relaix and Zammit, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about MuSC self-renewal.

claim: The myogenic regulatory factors including MYOD and MYOGENIN orchestrate MuSCs commitment and progression through the myogenic lineage
source: The myogenic regulatory factors including MYOD and MYOGENIN orchestrate MuSCs commitment and progression through the myogenic lineage (Wang et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about myogenic regulatory factors.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (CDKIs) are negative cell cycle regulators
source: Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (CDKIs) are negative cell cycle regulators.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CDKIs.

claim: CDKIs are divided into two structurally and functionally defined families: the INK4 family and the Cip/Kip family
source: CDKIs are divided into two structurally and functionally defined families: the INK4 family (including Cdkn2a, Cdkn2b, Cdkn2c, and Cdkn2d) and the Cip/Kip family (including Cdkn1a, Cdkn1b, and Cdkn1c) (Borriello et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about CDKI classification.

claim: Members of the Cip/Kip family have been shown to inhibit proliferation and promote differentiation in embryonic muscle or in myoblasts in vitro
source: Although members of the Cip/Kip family have been shown to inhibit proliferation and promote differentiation in embryonic muscle or in myoblasts in vitro, their involvement in postnatal MuSC cell cycle regulation is less well documented (Halevy et al., 1995; Reynaud et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 1999; Messina et al., 2005; Chakkalakal et al., 2014; Zalc et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about Cip/Kip family function in muscle.

claim: Cdkn1c is involved in stem cell quiescence
source: Given the emerging importance of Cdkn1c in stem cell quiescence (Matsumoto et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2011; Furutachi et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about Cdkn1c function in stem cell quiescence.

claim: Cdkn1c is involved in the early phase following MuSC activation events
source: we provide evidence that Cdkn1c is involved in the early phase following MuSC activation events
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic ablation of Cdkn1c leads to impaired muscle regeneration associated with decreased differentiation and increased proliferation
source: with its genetic ablation leading to impaired muscle regeneration associated with decreased differentiation and increased proliferation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figures 1-4.

claim: Cdkn1c is not detected in quiescent MuSCs but is induced upon activation and maintained in differentiating myogenic cells
source: We further show that Cdkn1c is not detected in quiescent MuSCs but is induced upon activation and maintained in differentiating myogenic cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Cdkn1c subcellular localization is specifically regulated during adult myogenesis, with a progressive cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation as activated myoblasts proceed to differentiation
source: Finally, we show that Cdkn1c subcellular localization is specifically regulated during adult myogenesis, with a progressive cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation as activated myoblasts proceed to differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5 and 6 showing localization changes.

claim: Muscle stem cells require Cdkn1c activity for the dynamic control of growth arrest during adult myogenesis
source: Our results suggest that muscle stem cells require Cdkn1c activity for the dynamic control of growth arrest during adult myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs express CDKN1b
source: Instead, it is established that they express CDKN1b, another member of the CDKI family including CDKN1c (Chakkalakal et al., 2014); our unpublished data].
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference and unpublished data.

claim: MYOD has been shown to induce Cdkn1c both by disrupting a chromatin loop to release the Cdkn1c promoter and by upregulating intermediate factors
source: Specifically, MYOD has been shown to induce Cdkn1c both by disrupting a chromatin loop to release the Cdkn1c promoter and by upregulating intermediate factors (Vaccarello et al., 2006; Figliola et al., 2008; Busanello et al., 2012; Battistelli et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MYOD regulation of Cdkn1c.

claim: A muscle-specific Cdkn1c regulatory element exists that MYOD binds and transactivates
source: Furthermore, we previously identified a muscle-specific Cdkn1c regulatory element that MYOD binds and transactivates (Zalc et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference from the authors' previous work.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation assays revealed direct CDKN1c-MYOD binding
source: while co-immunoprecipitation assays revealed direct CDKN1c-MYOD binding (Reynaud et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about protein-protein interaction.

claim: MyoD mutant mice present a similar muscle phenotype as Cdkn1c-deficient mice
source: Moreover, MyoD mutant mice present a similar muscle phenotype as our Cdkn1c-deficient mice (Megeney et al., 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference and comparison to the current study's findings.

claim: MYOD is expressed within hours after MuSC activation
source: MYOD is expressed within hours after MuSC activation (Zammit et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MYOD expression timing.

claim: MYOD sustains the transition from quiescence to cell cycle via the replication-related factor CDC6
source: and sustains the transition from quiescence to cell cycle via the replication-related factor CDC6 (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about MYOD function in cell cycle entry.

claim: MYOD induces growth arrest in non-myogenic cell lines
source: MYOD induces growth arrest in non-myogenic cell lines (Crescenzi et al., 1990; Sorrentino et al., 1990)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about MYOD function in cell cycle.

claim: MYOD has a well-established role for entry into the myogenic lineage
source: and has a well-established role for entry into the myogenic lineage.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about MYOD function.

claim: In dividing myoblasts MYOD activity is inhibited by Id proteins and CDK/Cyclin complexes
source: In fact, in dividing myoblasts MYOD activity is inhibited by Id proteins and CDK/Cyclin complexes (Wei and Paterson, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about MYOD regulation.

claim: Additional factors, including MYOGENIN, were suggested to initiate or enhance transcription of some MYOD targets
source: Furthermore, additional factors, including MYOGENIN, were suggested to initiate or enhance transcription of some MYOD targets (Blais et al., 2005; Cao et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about transcriptional regulation.

claim: CDKN1c could be implicated in cell cycle progression through CDK/Cyclin assembly, similarly to its Cip/Kip siblings
source: Firstly, CDKN1c could be implicated in cell cycle progression through CDK/Cyclin assembly, similarly to its Cip/Kip siblings (Michieli et al., 1994; Harper et al., 1995; LaBaer et al., 1997; Peschiaroli et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on cited references about Cip/Kip family function.

claim: In the absence of CDKN1a and CDKN1b, CDKN1c is solely responsible for CDK/Cyclin complex stabilization in mouse embryonic fibroblasts
source: In the absence of CDKN1a and CDKN1b, CDKN1c is solely responsible for CDK/Cyclin complex stabilization in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Cerqueira et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about CDKN1c function in MEFs.

claim: Cdkn1c-MYOD binding engages the CDKN1c helix domain that was found indispensable for CDK/Cyclin binding and inhibition
source: However, this might be less likely in myoblasts, where Cdkn1c-MYOD binding engages the CDKN1c helix domain (Reynaud et al., 2000) that was found indispensable for CDK/Cyclin binding and inhibition (Hashimoto et al., 1998; Reynaud et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about protein domain interactions.

claim: CDKN1c has been shown to interfere with the nuclear translocation of cyclin D1
source: CDKN1c has been shown to interfere with the nuclear translocation of cyclin D1 (Zou et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about CDKN1c function.

claim: CDKN1c can relocalize a fraction of CDK2 into the cytoplasm
source: and to relocalize a fraction of CDK2 into the cytoplasm (Figliola and Maione, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference about CDKN1c function.

claim: Cytoplasmic CDKN1c was described to regulate cell motility together with LIM-kinase1
source: Thirdly, while in the cytoplasm, CDKN1c might participate in MuSC mobilization, one of the earliest manifestations of their activation (Siegel et al., 2009). Cytoplasmic CDKN1c was described to regulate cell motility together with LIM-kinase1 (Vlachos and Joseph, 2009; Chow et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references about CDKN1c function in cell motility.

claim: CDKN1c plays essential roles at the initial phase following MuSC activation
source: In conclusion, our data indicate that CDKN1c plays essential roles at the initial phase following MuSC activation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: Cdkn1c mutants display a strong phenotype during the first days after injury in vivo
source: We suggest that CDKN1c acts at that early phase, as a) in vivo, Cdkn1c mutants display a strong phenotype during the first days after injury
evidence: The claim is supported by regeneration data from Figure 2 showing early defects.

claim: Cdkn1c mutant myoblasts have compromised functions in cultures that last a few days
source: and b) Cdkn1c mutant myoblasts have compromised functions in cultures that last a few days, thus resembling the first events after MuSC activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by myoblast culture data from Figure 3.

claim: CDKN1c presence is compatible with activation/proliferation and possibly represents an early activation event
